newsitem.title: UK: Cental banks' rethink; a dilemma for gold industry.
newsitem.headline: Cental banks' rethink; a dilemma for gold industry.

text.p: Fresh thinking by the world's central banks on how to manage their bullion reserves has created a major dilemma for the gold industry.
The banks have over 28,000 tonnes of gold sitting in their vaults and there were increasing signs they were not keen on holding on to it.
"It might not be true to say the banks have the industry at their mercy but there have to be changes as the realities of gold are appreciated," one commodities markets economist said.
That would inevitably lead to lower gold prices and fewer mines producing the metal.
This possibility suddenly loomed above the market last week when the Reserve Bank of Australia announced it had sold 167 tonnes of its gold reserves over the previous six months.
After some rumination the gold price, already weakened by the absence of investor interest and the threat of sales by the national banks, slumped to its lowest in almost 12 years.
Gold fixed at $320.60 per ounce on Friday up from the near 12-year low of $315.75 hit a couple of days earlier.

"There area a lot of frightened bulls out there. But really what is the point of owning something which pays no interest and is a hedge against something (inflation) that does not exist," asked Robin Aspinall, chief-economist at National Australia Bank.
The impact of future central banks sales -- and they are assumed to be inevitable -- will be variable.

"A central bank sale with a shock element will be much more damaging. There is no doubt the source (Australia) and rationale (asset review) last week was pretty shocking." said Tony Warwick-Ching, senior markets analyst at CRU International.
Australia is the world's third largest gold producer and its national bank has been criticised by gold miners at home and abroard for what they see as a breach of faith.

"Canada has been (selling from its reserves) for 20 years without causing the same uproar. It is unfortunate the Australian sale is taking place while sentiment is so bad. On a daily market basis 167 tonnes is not critical but shows a classic example of the market's vulnerability," said metal markets analyst Rhona O'Connell at stockbrokers T. Hoare and Co.
She added that unhedged producers in South Africa and Australia are definitely losing money at these prices. "A much as 57 percent of of western world gold production is now at a loss," she said.
The small Benoni God Mining Co in South Africa became the first casualty of the low price on Monday when its parent East Rand Propriety Mines announced it was stopping production.

"What is happening is that gold is being revalued to the market which shows that gold is not an asset apart because it has to perform," said precious metals markets analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
Smith estimated the cost of holding gold by the 12 central banks with the highest gold holdings was $15 billion a year in lost interest earnings.

"The days of investors in gold may be over. There has been a premium on gold and gold mining shares for years on the basis that the metal had special properties. Now we know it hasn't," an analyst said.
He was referring to the now discredited idea that gold commanded constant purchasing power. In other words, the ability to beat inflation.
"When logic comes in the price collapses to some new equilibrium. Logically the producers at the top of the price curve go away," said Smith.
CRU's Warwick-Ching said that probably central banks all over the world were doing the same cost-benefit analysis on their reserves and were coming to similar conclusions.
But whether or not there "would be a rush for the exits" as a result was debatable, he said.

UBS's Smith reasoned that a low price was not an issue for a central bank thinking of changing its reserve asset ratio by selling gold. "The banks are now as cunning and savvy as any investor and that is the problem," he said.

Due to the low book valuation of their reserves, The U.S., Japan, Germany and Switzerland could all sell at a profit even at current prices. Apart from Japan, all these major gold holding countries have indicated in the past few months that the value of their gold reserves are under examination, Smith noted.
"Another central bank sale would take the price to under $300 very quickly," one market analyst said.
Government permission would probably be needed before sales went ahead however.

"The reserve bank is formally responsible for the management of its external reserves so it could in principle make decisions on its own initiative, " said Robert Pringle, editor of the quarterly journal Central Banker.
"But the problem is the profit which has to be handed to the government. The question of the profit (of any sale) would be discussed between the central bank and the government," he said.
